This American showman, who co-founded a famous circus and peddled celebrated hoaxes, is often credited with 'there's a sucker born every minute' despite no proof he ever said it — who is it?
P. T. Barnum: American showman and politician (1810–1891)
The son of a freedman, this Roman emperor ruled for just 87 days in 193 AD before the Praetorian Guard killed him for trying to restore army discipline — who was he?
Pertinax: Roman emperor in 193. The son of a freedman, Pertinax rose from modest origins through a military career.
A Congress politician and former Governor of Rajasthan, she made history in 2007 as the first woman to become the President of India. Who is she?
Pratibha Patil: President of India from 2007 to 2012.
A Baptist minister and close friend of Martin Luther King Jr., he helped launch the Montgomery bus boycott and took over the SCLC after King's assassination. Who was he?
Ralph Abernathy: American activist and minister (1926–1990)
This Easy Company paratrooper earned the Distinguished Service Cross for his assault on Brécourt Manor during D-Day, and was later played by Damian Lewis in a hit HBO miniseries — who was he?
Richard Winters: United States Army officer and veteran (1918–2011)
This Japanese politician has served in the House of Councillors for the Liberal Democratic Party after stints as Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Defense and of the Cabinet Office — who is she?
This French economist and Green party lawmaker, representing a Paris constituency since 2022, became a leading voice of France's version of the Me Too movement — who is she?
Sandrine Rousseau: French economist and politician. Rousseau previously served as a vice-president of the University of Lille.

A close confidant of Vladimir Putin, this Russian official ran the Emergency Situations ministry for two decades before serving as Defence Minister and being tasked with supervising the war in Ukraine — who is he?
This king moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw and was the first Polish monarch from a Swedish royal house — who is he?
Sigismund III Vasa: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1587–1632), King of Sweden (1592–1599)

He out-debated and beat Abraham Lincoln for an 1858 Senate seat, then lost to him for the presidency two years later — and helped broker the Compromise of 1850 along the way. Which Illinois Democrat was he?
Stephen A. Douglas: American politician and lawyer (1813–1861)
Reigning over the Georgian Golden Age from 1184 to 1213, this Bagrationi monarch was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right and was given the title 'King' in medieval sources — who was she?
Tamar I: Queen of Georgia from 1184 to 1213. Tamar was successful in neutralizing this opposition and embarked on an energetic foreign policy aided by the decline of the hostile Seljuk Turks.

A protégé of Robert Walpole, this Whig statesman served as a Secretary of State for 30 unbroken years and dominated British foreign policy — and was twice Prime Minister. By which dukedom is he commonly known?
Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle: Prime Minister of Great Britain (1754–1756; 1757–1762)
This boy pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty undid his predecessor's experiment with worshipping a single sun-disk god and restored Egypt's traditional pantheon — who is he?
Tutankhamun: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1333 to 1324 BC.
Named for a queen who reigned from 1837 until 1901, this period saw the Irish Famine and the Crimean War against Russia — what was it called?
Victorian era: Queen Victoria's reign, 1837 to 1901.

Sparked by the 1791 Declaration of Pillnitz, this 1792–1797 conflict saw a loose alliance of European monarchies invade Revolutionary France, including the Duke of Brunswick's capture of Verdun — what was it called?
War of the First Coalition: 1792–1797 wars between France and European powers.
Born to mixed English-American parentage, this statesman led his nation through its darkest hour as Prime Minister during World War II. Who?
Winston Churchill: British statesman and writer (1874–1965)
This Central European nation emerged after World War I as a union of South Slavic peoples, survived until 1992, and was born from the merger of Serbia with a provisional state. What country was this?
Who among these four was born earliest?
William Osler (born 1849) is the earliest of the four. Osler created the first residency program for specialty training of physicians.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these four was born earliest?
George Grove (born 1820) is the earliest of the four. Grove was trained as a civil engineer, and successful in that profession, but his love of music drew him into musical administration.
Which of these four began earliest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt is an astronomer. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Augustus De Morgan is a mathematician. Augustus De Morgan (27 June 1806 – 18 March 1871) was a British mathematician and logician.
What is the atomic number of Technetium?
Technetium: Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
What is the atomic number of Sulfur?
Sulfur: Sulfur (American spelling or sulphur (Commonwealth spelling) is a chemical element; it has symbol S and atomic number 16.
In what year was Paul Allen born?
Paul Allen: Paul Gardner Allen (January 21, 1953 – October 15, 2018) was an American businessman, computer programmer, and investor.
In what year was Arthur Schopenhauer born?
Arthur Schopenhauer: Arthur Schopenhauer (22 February 1788 – 21 September 1860) was a German philosopher and writer.
In what year was Lex Fridman born?
Lex Fridman: Alexei "Lex" Fridman (born 15 August 1983) is an American computer scientist and podcaster.
In what year did Mario Molina die?
Mario Molina: Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez (19 March 1943 – 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
In what year did Edward Teller die?
Edward Teller: Born in Austria-Hungary in 1908, Teller emigrated to the US in the 1930s, one of the many so-called "Martians", a group of Hungarian scientist émigrés.
In what year was Möbius strip discovered?
Möbius strip: In mathematics, a Möbius strip, Möbius band, or Möbius loop is a surface that can be formed by attaching the ends of a strip of paper together with a half-twist.
R (programming language): Robert Gentleman. R is a programming language for statistical computing and data visualization.
Prunus domestica: People's Republic of China. Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae.
In which country is IAI Kfir?
Who is credited with discovering Eta Carinae?
Eta Carinae: Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser. It became the second-brightest star in the night sky between 11–14 March 1843 before fading well below naked-eye visibility after 1856.
Who is credited with discovering Benzene?
Benzene: Michael Faraday. Benzene is an organic chemical compound with the molecular formula C6H6.
Who is credited with discovering Vanadium?
Vanadium: Andrés Manuel del Río. Vanadium is a chemical element; it has symbol V and atomic number 23.

This British Formula One engineer, widely regarded as one of the sport's greatest designers, has served as technical chief at Williams, McLaren, and Red Bull, and now co-owns Aston Martin's F1 team — who is he?
Adrian Newey (born 26 December 1958) is a British engineer, aerodynamicist, automotive designer, and motorsport executive.

Caused by brain damage, disease, or sometimes sedative drugs, this condition splits into a retrograde type that erases memories before an event and an anterograde type that blocks new ones from forming — what is it called?
Amnesia is a deficit in memory caused by brain damage or brain diseases, but it can also be temporarily caused by the use of various sedative and hypnotic drugs.
Linked to smoking, high blood pressure and older age, this silent widening of the body's main artery to over 1.5 times normal size can suddenly rupture with severe abdominal pain — what condition?
Aortic aneurysm is an enlargement (dilatation) of the aorta to greater than 1.5 times normal size.

A professor at the University of North Carolina, this molecular biologist co-founded a foundation supporting Turkish students while researching DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, and circadian rhythms — who is he?
Aziz Sancar (born 8 September 1946) is a Turkish-American molecular biologist specializing in DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, and circadian clock.
Before TV stardom he was a Boeing mechanical engineer who invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then jumped to sketch comedy on Almost Live! — which science communicator?
Bill Nye (born November 27, 1955) is an American science communicator, television presenter, and former mechanical engineer.
This flowering plant family is known for flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, and includes crops ranging from leafy greens to root vegetables to condiment seeds. Name the family?
Brassicaceae (the older but equally valid) Cruciferae is a medium-sized and economically important family of flowering plants commonly known as the mustards, the crucifers, or the cabbage family.

Standing in contrast to the 'cat-like' carnivorans that diversified across Africa and southern Asia, this suborder unites dogs, bears, raccoons, and pinnipeds under one 'dog-like' umbrella — what's it called?
Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.

Appointed royal executioner under Louis XVI and later chief executioner of the First Republic, this Frenchman personally carried out the executions of the king, his queen, and Robespierre — who is he?
Charles-Henri Sanson (French; 15 February 1739 - 4 July 1806), was the royal executioner of France during the reign of King Louis XVI, and later chief executioner of the First French Republic.

Largely self-taught and grinding his own lenses from spare parts on a Kansas farm, this astronomer's homemade skills landed him at Lowell Observatory — where his 1930 survey turned up the first known body in the Kuiper belt; who was he?

Clyde Tombaugh (February 4, 1906 - January 17, 1997) was an American astronomer and telescope maker, best known for discovering Pluto in 1930, marking the first detection of what would eventually be recognized as the Kuiper belt.
Native to Europe and Western Asia, this birch-family shrub produces the round nuts sold commercially as hazelnuts — which species?
Corylus avellana is a species of flowering plant in the birch family Betulaceae.
Often called eczema, this umbrella term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness, and a rash, sometimes with small blisters or thickened skin — what is it?
Dermatitis is a term used for different types of skin inflammation, typically characterized by itchiness, redness and a rash.
Covering everything from a fibrous bone condition to a kidney disorder, this term for abnormal tissue growth is usually precancerous rather than outright malignant — what is it?

Dysplasia is any of various types of abnormal growth or development of cells (microscopic scale) or organs (macroscopic scale), and the abnormal histology or anatomical structure(s) resulting from such growth.
This tightly coiled duct sits behind each testicle, serving as the crucial link to the vas deferens where sperm mature before their onward journey — what is it?
Epididymis (pl.: epididymides or) is an elongated tubular genital organ attached to the posterior side of each one of the two male reproductive glands, the testicles.
This type of anaerobic metabolism harnesses the redox potential of reactants like glucose to produce ATP without needing oxygen. What process is it?
Fermentation is a type of anaerobic metabolism that harnesses the redox potential of the reactants to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and organic end products.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'milky,' this term names any gravity-bound system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter, ranging from tiny dwarfs to supergiants with a hundred trillion stars. What is it?
Galaxy is a system of stars, stellar remnants, interstellar gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity.
This week-long 2010 manhunt across Tyne and Wear and Northumberland ended when the fugitive shot himself following a six-hour standoff near Rothbury. What event is it?
Goose (pl.: geese) is a bird of any of several waterfowl species in the family Anatidae.

This now-outdated astronomical model placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the center of the universe, eventually replacing the geocentric view before itself being superseded by relativity — what model is it?
Heliocentrism (also known as the heliocentric model) is a superseded astronomical model that placed the Sun at the center of the universe, with the Earth and the planets in its orbit.
With atomic number 1, this element's most common isotope holds just one proton and one electron, and it's what stars like the Sun mainly burn — what is it?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
Many plants stockpile this energy-storing polysaccharide in their roots instead of starch, and doctors still use it as the benchmark substance for testing kidney function — name the fiber?
Inulin are a group of naturally occurring polysaccharides produced by many types of plants, industrially most often extracted from chicory.
This financier's 1999 bestseller on mutual funds became an investment classic after he founded a low-cost investing giant — who is he?

John C. Bogle (May 8, 1929 - January 16, 2019) was an American investor, business magnate and philanthropist who was the founder of The Vanguard Group and is credited with popularizing the index fund.
Named after the American endocrinologist who identified it in the 1940s, this chromosome anomaly, also called 47,XXY, typically affects phenotypic males with infertility. What condition is it?
Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosome anomaly.
Found in all land animals with internal skeletons, this fibrous band connects bones to other bones and, in birds and dinosaurs, secures flight feathers in place — what is it?
Ligament is a type of fibrous connective tissue in the body that connects bones to other bones.
Found in nearly every animal cell but rare in plants, this membrane-bound organelle acts as the cell's degradation center, breaking proteins, sugars, and fats into their building blocks — what is it?
Lysosome (/lassom/) is a membrane-bound organelle that is found in all animal cells (except red blood cells), and rarely in plant cells.

Awarded the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta, this German theoretical physicist is considered the originator of quantum theory and one of the founders of modern physics — who is he?
Max Planck (23 April 1858 - 4 October 1947) was a German theoretical physicist.
This dark-coated member of the weasel family comes in American and European species, plus an extinct 'sea' relative — what animal is it?

Mink are dark-coloured, semiaquatic, carnivorous mammals in the genera Mustela and Neogale and part of the family Mustelidae, which also includes weasels, stoats, martens, otters, badgers, and others.
Developed under a hypersonic flight program in the late 1990s, three single-use examples of this scramjet aircraft were built, the first destroyed in a 2001 test flight — which record holder is it?
NASA X-43 was an experimental unmanned hypersonic aircraft with multiple planned scale variations meant to test various aspects of hypersonic flight.
Containing turbinates and olfactory mucosa within its cavity, this organ centers the human face and provides an alternate airway while infants nurse — which body part?
Nose is a sensory organ and respiratory structure in vertebrates.
This bivalve mollusk is prized both as a delicacy on the half shell and, in certain species, for the pearls it produces inside its shell — what is it?
Oyster is the common name for a number of different families of salt-water bivalve molluscs that live in marine or brackish habitats.

Which American chemist was the first to synthesize physostigmine and pioneered making progesterone and testosterone from plant sterols — even starting a company to extract steroid intermediates from wild Mexican yams?
Percy Lavon Julian (April 11, 1899 - April 19, 1975) was an American research chemist and a pioneer in the chemical synthesis of medicinal drugs from plants.

Despite its fearsome reputation as a ferocious predator, this South American freshwater fish actually eats a varied diet that includes plant material, making it more omnivore than monster — what fish is it?
Piranha (or) is any of a number of freshwater fish species in the subfamily Serrasalminae, of the family Serrasalmidae, in the order Characiformes.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.

Named for the ragged appearance of its leaves, this genus of flowering plants native mainly to North America has become an invasive nuisance in parts of Europe due to climate change — what plant is it?
Ragweed are flowering plants in the genus Ambrosia in the aster family, Asteraceae.

Usually hidden below the soil surface but sometimes growing aerial or aerating instead, these plant organs anchor a plant while drawing in the water and nutrients it needs to grow taller and faster — name them?
Root are the organs of a plant that are modified to provide anchorage for the plant and take in water and nutrients into the plant body, which allows plants to grow taller and faster.

These colorful predatory marine animals — single polyps usually anchored by their base — are named after a terrestrial flower and, unlike their jellyfish relatives, skip the medusa stage entirely; what are they?
Sea anemone (-) are a group of predatory marine invertebrate animals constituting the order Actiniaria.
Famous for their slowness, these tree-dwelling Neotropical mammals are closest relatives of anteaters and come in just seven living species across two genera — what are they?
Sloth are a Neotropical group of xenarthran mammals constituting the suborder Folivora, including the extant arboreal tree sloths and extinct terrestrial ground sloths.
Director of research at Cambridge's Centre for Theoretical Cosmology, he was the Lucasian Professor of Mathematics from 1979 to 2009. Who?

Stephen Hawking (8 January 1942 - 14 March 2018) was an English theoretical astrophysicist, cosmologist, and author who was director of research at the Centre for Theoretical Cosmology at the University of Cambridge.
A staple corm across African, Caribbean, Oceanian, and Asian cultures, this root vegetable of the arum family is often likened to yams — what is it?
Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.

Founding pastor of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in New York City and co-founder of Redeemer City to City, this American theologian wrote the bestsellers The Reason for God and The Prodigal God — who was he?
Tim Keller (pastor) (September 23, 1950 - May 19, 2023) was an American Presbyterian pastor, Reformed theologian, and Christian apologist.
Lined with a type of tissue called transitional epithelium, this narrow tube can develop kidney stones or reflux problems and connects each kidney to the bladder — what is it?
Ureter are tubes composed of smooth muscle that transport urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.
He co-developed the V-2 at Peenemünde — the first artificial object to cross the Kármán line into space — before bringing his rocketry to the United States; who was this engineer?
Wernher von Braun (23 March 1912 - 16 June 1977) was a German American aerospace engineer and space architect.
Also called motor neuron disease or Lou Gehrig's disease, this terminal condition progressively destroys the neurons that control voluntary muscle movement — what is it?
Nicknamed the painted hunter for its mottled coat, this sub-Saharan canine hunts cooperatively at dawn and dusk and is the only living member of its genus, Lycaon — which species?
African wild dog: Species of canine. The African wild dog (Lycaon pictus), also called painted dog and Cape hunting dog, is a wild canine native to sub-Saharan Africa.
With more than 1,100 species including onions, garlic, leeks, and chives, this is the largest genus in the flowering plant family Amaryllidaceae — which genus?
Allium: Genus of flowering plants. The flowers form an umbel at the top of a leafless stalk.
This cosmopolitan family of water birds, found on every continent but Antarctica, groups together the ducks, geese, and swans — what is it?
Anatidae: Biological family of water birds. The family has a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on all the world's continents except Antarctica.
This psychological state describes a lack of feeling, motivation, or concern, sitting on a spectrum between normal drive and akinetic mutism — what is it called?
Apathy: State of indifference, or the suppression of emotions.

First catalogued in 1729 by an Italian priest who thought its spore-forming structures resembled a holy-water sprinkler, this genus of several hundred mold species takes its name from the Latin word for 'to sprinkle' — which genus?
Aspergillus: Genus of fungi. Aspergillus is a genus consisting of several hundred mold species found in various climates worldwide.
Named from a Greek word meaning 'heavy,' this soft silvery alkaline earth metal with atomic number 56 wasn't isolated until 1808 via electrolysis, decades after being identified — which element?
Barium: Chemical element with atomic number 56 (Ba)
Produced continuously by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, this yellow-green fluid is released into the small intestine to help digest fats — what is it?
Bile: Dark greenish-brown fluid aiding in the digestion of fats.

Developed in the 1980s-90s to replace an aging Cold War transport aircraft, this large military cargo plane carries forward the name of two earlier piston-engined predecessors, the C-74 and C-124. What is this modern behemoth called?
Boeing C-17 Globemaster III: American four engine military transport aircraft.

Affecting roughly 22% of people worldwide, this oral parafunctional habit — often during sleep and without the person's awareness — can leave you with aching jaw muscles, headaches, and worn-down teeth. What is it?
Bruxism: Grinding or clenching of the teeth.
When this yeast infection strikes the mouth it's commonly called thrush, leaving telltale white patches on the tongue — what is the condition?
Candidiasis: Fungal infection due to any type of Candida.
Responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide in 2020, this condition clouds the eye's lens and causes halos around lights — which condition?
Cataract: Clouding of the lens inside the eye, causing poor vision.
Named for both the tree and its edible nut, this genus of temperate deciduous trees belongs to the beech family — what is it?
Chestnut: Genus of plants. The name also refers to the edible nuts they produce.
Homologous with the male foreskin and developing as part of the labia minora, which fold of skin surrounds and protects the tip of the clitoris?
Clitoral hood: Part of the vulva that covers and protects the glans of the clitoris.
The largest living bird species, this flightless native of Africa is one of just two living species in its genus — which bird?
Common ostrich: Species of flightless bird. The common ostrich is one of two extant species of ostriches, the only living members of the genus Struthio in the ratite group of birds.
Found mainly in muscle and brain tissue, which organic compound helps recycle ATP — its phosphorylated form donating phosphate to ADP to regenerate the body's energy currency?
Creatine: Chemical compound. Creatine ( or) is an organic compound that, in vertebrates, facilitates recycling of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), primarily in muscle and brain tissue.
Most genera in this family of armored, burrowing mammals are extinct — only one genus survives today, with eight living species — which family?

This widely used polar aprotic solvent dissolves both polar and nonpolar compounds, mixes with water, and — once absorbed through the skin — leaves a curious garlic-like taste in the mouth. Which organosulfur compound is it?
Dimethyl sulfoxide: Organosulfur chemical compound used as a solvent.

This movement disorder causes involuntary muscle contractions that twist the body into abnormal postures, and can sometimes be treated with botulinum toxin injections or deep brain stimulation — what is it?
Dystonia: Neurological movement disorder. Dystonia is often intensified or exacerbated by physical activity, and symptoms may progress into adjacent muscles.
Caused by viruses like herpes simplex or rabies, this inflammation of the brain can bring fever, confusion, and a stiff neck — what is this condition?

Encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain. The severity can be variable with symptoms including reduction or alteration in consciousness, aphasia, headache, fever, confusion, a stiff neck, and vomiting.
This complex-analysis identity states that e raised to the power of ix equals cosine x plus i times sine x, linking exponential and trigonometric functions — what is it called?
Euler's formula: Complex exponential in terms of sine and cosine. The formula is still valid if x is a complex number, and is also called Euler's formula in this more general case.
This Stanford computer scientist built ImageNet, the vast labeled dataset that ignited the deep-learning revolution in computer vision in the 2010s. Who is she?
Also called vitamin B9, this essential nutrient the body can't make itself is vital for building DNA and RNA — which is why its synthetic form, folic acid, is added to fortified foods. What is it?
Folate: Vitamin B9; nutrient essential for DNA synthesis. Folate, also known as vitamin B9 and folacin, is one of the B vitamins.
Caused by a loss of blood supply and marked by skin turning red or black, this condition comes in dry, wet, and gas forms — what is it?
Gangrene: Type of tissue death by ischemia.
Found in birds, crocodilians, and earthworms alike, this thick-muscled digestive organ grinds food with the help of swallowed grit — what's it called?
Gizzard: Digestive organ of some animals.

Once classified as a subfamily of the seabasses, this diverse family of marine ray-finned fish is now treated as distinct, with most members drawn from two large genera. What are they commonly called?
Grouper: Family of fishes. The common name "grouper" is usually given to fish in one of two large genera: Epinephelus and Mycteroperca.
About the size of a closed fist and enclosed in a protective sac called the pericardium, this four-chambered organ sits in the chest between the lungs and pumps blood through the body — which organ?
Heart: Organ found in humans and other animals.
Named for the English physician who first described it in 1832, this cancer is defined by multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes — what is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of blood and immune-system cancer.
Named from Greek words meaning "over" and "formation," this condition enlarges tissue by increasing the number of cells rather than their size — which term, distinct from hypertrophy?
Hyperplasia: Enlargement of tissue due to cell proliferation.
Commonly known as chaga, this parasitic fungus grows on birch trees and forms a charcoal-like black mass often marketed, questionably, as a health supplement — what's its scientific name?
Inonotus obliquus: Species of fungus. Inonotus obliquus, commonly called chaga (a Latinization of the Russian word ча́га), is a fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.
The first woman to chair the Federal Reserve, this American economist later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — who is she?
Janet Yellen: American economist and government official (born 1946)
Named the type genus of the walnut family, this group of deciduous trees produces the walnuts eaten worldwide, with China responsible for half the global supply — which genus?
Juglans: Genus of trees. Walnut trees are any species of tree in the plant genus Juglans, the type genus of the family Juglandaceae, the seeds of which are referred to as walnuts.
Named from a Wiradjuri word imitating its own call, this Australian tree kingfisher's cackling laugh is a go-to sound effect for movie jungle scenes — what is it?
Kookaburra: Genus of birds (terrestrial tree kingfishers)
Also known as Peruvian ginseng, this Andean root crop is grown at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and exported worldwide as a dietary powder — what plant is it?
Lepidium meyenii: Plant species native to South America.
This American WWII twin-engine, twin-boom fighter carried its pilot alone in a central nacelle and served as fighter-bomber, night fighter, and long-range escort — which aircraft was it?
Lockheed P-38 Lightning: American twin-engined fighter of WWII. The Lockheed P-38 Lightning is an American single-seat, twin-engined fighter aircraft that was used during World War II.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Widely brewed as a calming herbal tea despite limited clinical evidence for its effects, this annual plant in the daisy family goes by the nickname 'scented mayweed' — which plant?
Matricaria chamomilla: Species of flowering plant.
Once made by roasting wood — hence its old name 'wood alcohol' — this simplest alcohol smells much like the drinkable kind but is far more poisonous. What is it?

Also called 'selective sound sensitivity syndrome,' this disorder causes specific sounds to trigger strong negative emotional and physiological reactions, though it isn't yet listed in the DSM-5-TR — what is it called?
Misophonia: Disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds.
Native to the Americas from Texas down to Argentina, this domesticated waterfowl species has also gone feral in New Zealand, Australia, and parts of Europe — which species?
Muscovy duck: Species of bird. The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
Named after a German physical chemist, this electrochemistry formula calculates a reaction's reduction potential from temperature, electron count, and reactant concentrations — which relationship?
Nernst equation: Physical law in electrochemistry.
Built from a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group, these molecules are the monomer building blocks of DNA and RNA — what are they called?
Nucleotide: Biological molecules constituting nucleic acids.

Believed to be the world's fourth-leading cause of disability, this degenerative joint disease comes from the breakdown of cartilage and bone, often striking the fingertips, thumb base, knees, and hips — what is it?
Osteoarthritis: Form of arthritis caused by degeneration of joints.
Known as the passion flower, this genus of about 550 species also has ornamental hybrids that have won Royal Horticultural Society awards and varieties used in ayahuasca analogs — name the genus?
Passiflora: Genus of flowering plants in the passion flower family.
Called the 'father of transplantation,' this Brazilian-born biologist won a 1960 Nobel for his work on acquired immune tolerance and graft rejection — who was he?
This imperial and US customary unit of volume is exactly one-eighth of a gallon, though the British version is about 20% larger than its American counterpart — which unit?

Pint: Unit of volume in the imperial and US systems. The pint (symbol pt, sometimes abbreviated as p) is a unit of volume or capacity in both the imperial and United States customary measurement systems.
Also called caustic potash and written KOH, this dangerously corrosive white solid is a prototypical strong base and the key precursor to most liquid and soft soaps — which compound?
Potassium hydroxide: Inorganic compound (KOH). It has many industrial and niche applications, most of which utilize its caustic nature and its reactivity toward acids.

This deep-sea fish off Australia and New Zealand has almost no muscle and a gelatinous body just under water's density, letting it float effortlessly at depths beyond 600 meters — what is its scientific name?
Psychrolutes marcidus: Species of fish. Psychrolutes marcidus, the smooth-head blobfish, or simply the blobfish, is a deep-sea fish of the family Psychrolutidae.
Chairman of a sprawling Indian conglomerate from 1991 to 2012, this architecture graduate of Cornell received both the Padma Bhushan and the Padma Vibhushan. Who was he?
Ratan Tata: Indian industrialist and philanthropist (1937–2024)
Recognizable by its long, black-and-white ringed tail, this highly social Madagascar primate lives in troops of up to 30 and is dominated by females — which species?
Ring-tailed lemur: Species of mammal from Madagascar.
A Stanford physicist who joined NASA in 1978, she became the first American woman in space in 1983 — and, at 32, the youngest American to fly there. Who is she?
